claim: Robert Fortune says the East India Company's Court of Directors sent him to China to obtain the finest tea plants, native manufacturers and implements for the Government tea plantations in the Himalayas; he left Southampton on 20 June 1848.

evidence.quote: deputed by the Honourable the Court of Directors of the East India Company to proceed to China for the purpose of obtaining the finest varieties of the Tea-plant
On the 20th of June, 1848, I left Southampton

claim: Fortune claims that upwards of twenty thousand tea plants, eight first-rate manufacturers and a large supply of implements were taken from China's best tea districts and conveyed safely to the Himalayas.

evidence.quote: Upwards of twenty thousand tea-plants, eight first-rate manu- facturers, and a large supply of implements were procured from the finest tea-districts of China

note: Self-reported by Fortune; attribute it ('Fortune wrote'). Not audited against Company records in this run.

claim: To travel inland Fortune wore Chinese dress and had his queue ('tail') dressed by a barber.

evidence.quote: My servants now procured me a Chinese dress, and had the tail which I had worn in former years nicely dressed by the barber.

note: Human detail. Do not call it a 'theft' or 'spying' in his words; he does not.

claim: Fortune left Shanghai with the manufacturers and sixteen glazed cases of plants and seeds on 16 February 1851 and reached Calcutta on 15 March 1851.

evidence.quote: which now filled sixteen glazed cases
This was on the 16th of February, 1851.
arrived at Calcutta on the 15th of March.

claim: Fortune's plants were for the north-western Himalaya: he describes the Company's tea farm at Hawulbaugh, about six miles north-west of Almora in Kumaon, at about 4500 feet, and the plantations of Garhwal and Kumaon.

evidence.quote: This tea-farm is situated on the banks of the river Kosilla, about six miles north-west from Almorah, the capital of Kumaon.
It is about 4500 feet above the level of the sea.

note: His book says nothing of Darjeeling (grep: 0 hits); do not put Darjeeling on his route from this source.

claim: On 24 December 1834 the Company's Committee of Tea Culture told the Governor General that the tea shrub is 'beyond all doubt indigenous in Upper Assam', crediting Capt. Jenkins and Lieut. Charlton.

evidence.locator: p. 42-43, Committee letter, para 2, djvu lines ~28-36
evidence.quote: the tea shrub is beyond all doubt indigenous in Upper Assam
Calcutta, Dec. 24, 1834. Signed by the Committee of Tea Culture.

method: method/tea_numbers.py: 1848-1834 = 14 years before Fortune set out.
note: The same letter says David Scott sent leaves from Manipur in 1826, and the editor's note gives earlier sightings (Wilcox; Grant and Pemberton 1828). So 1834 is official recognition, not first contact.

claim: Before the British recognised it, the Singphos and Khamtis of Upper Assam already drank an infusion of the leaves, which they cut, boiled, squeezed into a ball and dried in the sun (Lieut. Charlton, 17 May 1834).

evidence.locator: p. 46, Charlton to Jenkins, 17 May 1834, djvu lines ~263-266
evidence.quote: The Singphos and Kamtees are in the habit of drinking an in- fusion of the leaves

note: Charlton reports this second-hand ('I have lately understood'). Say 'a British officer wrote in 1834 that...'.

claim: In 2024-25 (FINAL) Assam produced 666.82 million kg of India's 1,315.77 million kg of tea: 50.7%, about half (our measurement).

evidence.locator: TEA PRODUCTION IN 2024-25 (APR-MAR)- FINAL, Total column, rows Assam and All India

note: Production by region is not production by plant variety: this does not show which variety Assam's bushes are.

claim: The Committee in 1834 believed the Assam plant was 'the identical tea of China', not a separate kind.

evidence.quote: the identical tea of China, which is the exclusive source of all the varieties and shades of the tea of commerce

note: Modern 'var. assamica' classification NOT checked in this run (lite cap).

claim: The Bohea black-tea town Tsong-gan-hien (27 47' 38" N, per Fortune citing Jesuit observations) and Manche, a Khamti village east of Sadiya where Wilcox was shown a tea tree (27 29' 16" N), lie only about 34 km apart in latitude (our measurement).

evidence.locator: Ch. on Bohea hills, djvu line ~10094

evidence.quote: writes from Manché, a Khamti village

note: Latitude only; no longitude for Tsong-gan-hien in S01, so no east-west distance.

claim: Darjeeling district produced 5.75 million kg in 2024-25 (FINAL), 0.44% of India; Assam made about 116 times as much (our measurement).
note: Context only; Fortune's book does not link his plants to Darjeeling.
